==English==
{{wp}}

===Etymology===
From {{inh|en|enm|slaw}}, {{m|enm|slow}}, from {{inh|en|ang|slāw|t=lazy; inert, slow}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*slaiw}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*slaiwaz|t=blunt; dull; exhausted, faint, sluggish, weak, weary; listless, torpid; dim-witted, slow; lazy, slack}}, possibly from {{der|en|ine-pro|*(s)leyH-|*sleyH-u-|bad}}.
{{col-top|2|cog}}
Cognate with {{cog|nl|slee}}, {{m|nl|sleeuw|t=cramped, stiff; blunt; sour}}, {{cog|da|sløv|t=blunt; dull; apathetic, lethargic, listless, sluggish, torpid; drowsy}}, {{cog|is|sljór|t=dim-witted; blunt; jaded}}, {{cog|nn|sljo}}, {{m|nn|slø}}, {{m|nn|sløv|t=blunt; weak; lazy}}, {{cog|sv|slö|t=dull; lazy, lethargic, slow, sluggish}}.
{{col-bottom}}

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/sləʊ/|a=UK}}
** {{audio|en|En-uk-slow.ogg|a=UK}}
** {{IPA|en|/slaː/|a=Northumbria}}
* {{IPA|en|/sloʊ/|a=US}}

* {{rhymes|en|əʊ|s=1}}
* {{homophones|en|sloe}}

===Adjective===
{{en-adj|er}}

# Taking a long [[time]] to move or go a short [[distance]], or to perform an action; not [[quick]] in [[motion]]; [[proceed]]ing at a [[low]] speed.
#: {{ux|en|a '''slow''' train;  a '''slow''' computer}}
#: {{ux|en|Why were you so '''slow''' to answer my question?}}
#: {{ux|en|Turkey should always be cooked in a [[slow oven|'''slow''' oven]].}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-07-20|volume=408|issue=8845
|title=[http://www.economist.com/news/http://www.economist.com/news/business/21582001-army-new-online-courses-scaring-wits-out-traditional-universities-can-they The attack of the MOOCs]
|passage=Dotcom mania was '''slow''' in coming to higher education, but now it has the venerable industry firmly in its grip. Since the launch early last year of Udacity and Coursera, two Silicon Valley start-ups offering free education through MOOCs, massive open online courses, the ivory towers of academia have been shaken to their foundations.}}
# Not happening in a short time; [[spread]] over a comparatively long time.
#* {{RQ:Milton Paradise Lost|lines=692–695|sig=[Mm3]|verso=1|page=279|text=Theſe changes in the Heav’ns, though '''ſlow''', produc’d / Like change on Sea and Land, ſideral blaſt, / Vapour, and Miſt, and Exhalation hot, / Corrupt and Peſtilent: {{...}}}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|year=2013|month=May–June|author=[http://www.americanscientist.org/authors/detail/charles-t-ambrose Charles T. Ambrose]
|title=[http://www.americanscientist.org/issues/feature/2013/3/alzheimerrsquos-disease-the-great-morbidity-of-the-21st-century Alzheimer’s Disease]
|volume=101|issue=3|page=200|magazine=w:American Scientist
|passage=Similar studies of rats have employed four different intracranial resorbable, '''slow''' sustained release systems—surgical foam, a thermal gel depot, a microcapsule or biodegradable polymer beads.}}
# {{lb|en|informal|somewhat|derogatory}} Of [[reduce]]d [[intellectual]] [[capacity]]; not quick to [[comprehend]].
#* {{quote-journal|en|year=1960|work=Dissertation Abstracts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hyAhAQAAMAAJ|volume=20|page=4007|passage=Experienced classroom teachers are well acquainted with the attention-seeker, the shy girl, the aggressive boy, the poor concentrator, the '''slow''' student,{{nb...}}}}
# Not [[hasty]]; not tending to [[hurry]]; acting with [[deliberation]] or caution.
#* {{RQ:KJV|Proverbs|xiv|29|passage=He that is '''slow''' to wrath is of great understanding.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1999|author=Brian Paul Kaufman; K. Winston Caine|title=Prayer, Faith, and Healing: Cure Your Body, Heal Your Mind and Restore Your Soul|passage=And even after the emotional cast comes off, we need to be '''slow''' about getting deeply involved in a relationship again.}}
# {{lb|en|of a [[clock]] or the like}} [[behind|Behind]] in time; indicating a time [[early|earlier]] than the [[true]] time.
#: {{ux|en|That clock is '''slow'''.}}
# Lacking [[spirit]]; [[deficient]] in [[liveliness]] or [[briskness]].
# {{lb|en|of a period of time}} Not [[busy]]; lacking [[activity]].
#: {{ux|en|It was a '''slow''' news day, so the editor asked us to make our articles wordier.}}
#: {{ux|en|I'm just sitting here with a desk of cards, enjoying a '''slow''' afternoon.}}

==English==

===Etymology===
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:also|tree=1}}
{{root|en|ine-pro|*h₂el-|id=all}}{{word|en|ine|swé}}
From {{inh|en|enm|also}}, {{m|enm|alswo}}, {{m|enm|alswa}} (also {{m|enm|als|als(e)}}, {{m|enm|as}}, whence English {{m|en|as}}), from {{inh|en|ang|eallswā||just like, also}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*allswā}}, equivalent to {{com|en|all|so}}. Cognate with {{cog|sco|alsa}}, {{m|sco|alswa||also, even so, in the same way, as, as well}}, {{cog|stq|also||accordingly, therefore, thus}}, {{cog|fy|alsa||so, just so, even so, thus}}, {{cog|osx|alsō||similarly, as if, just as, when}}, {{cog|nl|alzo||so, thus}}, {{cog|de|also||so, thus}}, {{cog|da|altså||so}}, {{cog|nb|altså||so, therefore, accordingly, thus}}, {{cog|nn|altso||so, accordingly, therefore, thus}}, {{cog|sv|alltså||so, therefore, accordingly, thus, then}}. {{doublet|en|as}}. More at {{m|en|all}}, {{m|en|so}}.

===Adverb===
{{en-adv|-}}

# {{lb|en|conjunctive|focus}} [[in addition|In addition]]; [[besides]]; [[as well]]; [[further]]; [[too]]. {{defdate|from 14<sup>th</sup> c.}}
#: {{ux|en|Everyone had eggs for breakfast, but Alice '''also''' had toast. '''Also''', she finished hers in under half an hour.}}
#: {{ux|en|'''Also''' common are languages, like Latin, with a [[three-way]] distinction (''proximal, medial and distal'').}}
#: {{ux|en|When you withdraw yor forces, we shall '''also''' withdraw ours.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|year=1905|author=Bertrand Russell|journal=On Denoting
|passage=The subject of denoting is of very great importance, not only in logic and mathematics, but '''also''' in the theory of knowledge.}}
#* {{RQ:Belloc Lowndes Lodger|I|0016
|passage=Thus the red damask curtains which now shut out the fog-laden, drizzling atmosphere of the Marylebone Road, had cost a mere song, and yet they might have been warranted to last another thirty years. A great bargain '''also''' had been the excellent Axminster carpet which covered the floor;{{nb...}}.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|year=2013|month=May-June|author=[http://www.americanscientist.org/authors/detail/katrina-g-claw Katrina G. Claw]
|title=[http://www.americanscientist.org/issues/feature/2013/3/rapid-evolution-in-eggs-and-sperm Rapid Evolution in Eggs and Sperm]
|volume=101|issue=3|magazine=w:American Scientist
|passage=Many genes with reproductive roles '''also''' have antibacterial and immune functions, which indicate that the threat of microbial attack on the sperm or egg may be a major influence on rapid evolution during reproduction.}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} To the same [[degree]] or [[extent]]; [[so]], [[as]].
#* {{quote-book|en|year=c. 1709|author=w:John Strype|title=Annals of the Reformation and Establishment of Religion
|passage={{...}} thereupon the queen's majesty {{...}} did send a solemn ambassade of her privy-counsellors, whereof one was an ancient earl of the realm, the other '''also''' an ancient baron of the same, and others of the council of her state {{...}}}}

====Usage notes====
The adverb '''also''' can go in various places within a sentence, with minimal change of meaning.
*{{ux|en|The golf courses are excellent. '''Also''', the tennis courts are fantastic.}}
*{{ux|en|The golf courses are excellent and the tennis courts are fantastic '''also'''.}}
*{{ux|en|Not only are the golf courses excellent but '''also''' the tennis courts are fantastic.}}
*{{ux|en|There are not just excellent golf courses here. There are '''also''' fantastic tennis courts.}}

In Norwegian non-native English, may be used in the beginning of sentence, because of confusing with the {{m+|nb|altså}} and {{m+|nn|altso}}.

===Etymology 1===
{{etymon|en|id=rule|:inh|enm:lawe|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|lawe}}, {{m|enm|laȝe}}, from {{inh|en|ang|lagu|t=law}}, borrowed from {{der|en|non|lǫg|t=law|lit=things laid down or firmly established}}, originally the plural of {{m|non|lag||layer, stratum, a laying in order, measure, stroke}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*lagą|t=that which is laid down}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*legʰ-|t=to lie}}. Cognate with {{cog|sco|law|t=law}}, {{cog|is|lög|t=things laid down, law}}, {{cog|fo|lóg|t=law}}, {{cog|no|lov|t=law}}, {{cog|sv|lag|t=law}}, {{cog|da|lov|t=law}}, {{cog|fi|laki|t=law}}. Compare typologically distant cognate {{m+|ru|уложе́ние}}. Displaced native {{noncog|ang|ǣ}} and {{m|ang|ġesetnes}}. More at {{l|en|lay}}.

Not typically thought to be related to {{m|en|legal}}, nor to {{ncog|fr|loi}}, {{ncog|es|ley}}, as these all derive from {{ncog|la|lēx}}, ultimately from {{ncog|ine-pro|*leǵ-|t=to gather}}; however, see {{l|la|lēx}} for an alternative theory that indeed links it to the same {{m+|ine-pro|*legʰ-}}. In any case, {{m-self|en|law}} is the inherited {{w|Germanic}} term whereas {{m|en||leg-}} is {{lg|borrowed}} via Latin and {{cog|roa|-}}.

===Etymology 1===
From {{inh|en|enm|flag}}, {{m|enm|flagge||flag}}, further etymology {{unc|en|nocap=1}}. Perhaps from or related to early {{der|en|enm|flage}} {{gloss|name for a baby's garment}} and {{der|en|ang|flagg}}, {{m|ang|flacg||[[cataplasm]], [[poultice]], [[plaster]]}}.  Or, perhaps ultimately {{onomatopoeic|en|title=imitative}}, or otherwise drawn from {{der|en|gem-pro|*flaką|t=something flat}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*pleh₂-||flat, broad, plain}}, referring to the shape.<ref name = harper>{{R:Online Etymology Dictionary|flag}}</ref>

Germanic cognates include Saterland Frisian {{m|stq|Flaage||flag}}, West Frisian {{m|fy|flagge||flag}}, Dutch {{m|nl|vlag||flag}}, {{cog|de|Flagge||flag}}, {{cog|sv|flagga||flag}}, {{cog|da|flag||flag, ship's flag}}. Compare also {{cog|enm|flacken||to flutter, palpitate}}, {{cog|sv|-}} dialectal {{m|sv|flage||to flutter in the wind}}, {{cog|non|flögra||to flap about}}. Akin to {{cog|goh|flogarōn||to flutter}}, {{cog|goh|flogezen||to flutter, flicker}}, {{cog|enm|flakeren||to move quickly to and fro}}, {{cog|ang|flacor||fluttering, flying}}. #* {{quote-book|en|year=1994|author=John Ratcliffe|title=Foundations of Hyperbolic Manifolds|url=https://books.google.com.au/books?id=kvTiBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA230&dq=%22flag%22%7C%22flags%22+polytope&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwiEtu_XuPfMAhUC3mMKHewGAuQQ6AEIcDAN#v=onepage&q=%22flag%22%7C%22flags%22%20polytope&f=false|page=230|passage=A '''''flag''''' of ''P'' is a sequence (''F<sub>0</sub>, F<sub>1</sub>, ..., F<sub>m</sub>'') of faces of ''P'' such that dim ''F<sub>i</sub>'' = ''i'' for each ''i'' and ''F<sub>i</sub>'' is a side of ''F''<sub>''i''+1</sub> for each ''i'' < ''m''.{{...}}A ''regular polytope'' in ''X'' is a polytope ''P'' in ''X'' whose group of symmetries in <''P''> acts transitively on its '''flags'''.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2002|author=Peter McMullen; Egon Schulte|title=Abstract Regular Polytopes|publisher=Encyclopedia of Mathematics and Its Applications 92|pageurl=https://books.google.com.au/books?id=JfmlMYe6MJgC&pg=PA31&dq=%22flag%22%7C%22flags%22+polytope&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwiEtu_XuPfMAhUC3mMKHewGAuQQ6AEIKjAA#v=onepage&q=%22flag%22%7C%22flags%22%20polytope&f=false|page=31
|passage=We call ''P'' (''combinatorially'') ''regular'' if its automorphism group ''Γ''(''P'') is transitive on its '''flags'''.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2006|author=Peter McMullen; Egon Schulte|chapter=Regular and Chiral Polytopes in Low Dimensions|editors=Harold Scott Macdonald Coxeter; Chandler Davis; Erich W. Ellers|title=The Coxeter Legacy: Reflections and Projections|pageurl=https://books.google.com.au/books?id=cKpBGcqpspIC&pg=PA91&dq=%22flag%22%7C%22flags%22+polytope&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwiEtu_XuPfMAhUC3mMKHewGAuQQ6AEIazAM#v=onepage&q=%22flag%22%7C%22flags%22%20polytope&f=false|page=91
|passage=Roughly speaking, chiral polytopes have half as many possible automorphisms as have regular polytopes. More technically, the ''n''-polytope ''P'' is ''chiral'' if it has two orbits of '''flags''' under its group ''Γ''(''P''), with adjacent '''flags''' in different orbits.}}
# {{lb|en|mathematics|linear algebra}} A sequence of [[subspace]]s of a [[vector space]], beginning with the [[null]] space and ending with the vector space itself, such that each member of the sequence (until the last) is a [[proper]] subspace of the next.

* {{IPA|en|/ˈdɪvɪdɛnd/}}
* {{audio|en|en-us-dividend.ogg|a=US}}

===Noun===
{{en-noun}}

# {{lb|en|finance}} A [[cash]] [[payment]] of [[money]] by a [[company]] to its [[shareholder]]s, usually made [[periodically]] (e.g., [[quarterly]] or [[annually]]).
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1861|title=Laws of Pennsylvania of the Session of 1861|pageurl=https://books.google.com/books?id=MhNAAAAAYAAJ&dq=%22twelve%20per%20centum%22&pg=PA511#v=onepage&q&f=false|page=511
|passage=On all '''dividends''' which do not exceed six per centum per annum, eight per centum; on '''dividends''' exceeding six per centum and not exceeding seven per centum, a tax of nine per centum...}}
#* {{RQ:en:CNN|author=Paul R. La Monica|title=As markets wobble, buy the stocks that pay you back|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2022/09/14/investing/stocks-dividends-yield-income|date=2022-09-14|passage=Quarterly or annual '''dividend''' payments provide good income streams for investors who need cash in the short-term. And for those playing the longer game, '''dividends''' can be reinvested to buy even more shares in those same companies.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20250724175551/https://edition.cnn.com/2022/09/14/investing/stocks-dividends-yield-income|archivedate=24 July 2025}}
# {{lb|en|arithmetic}} A number or [[expression]] that is to be divided by another.
#: {{ux|en|In "42 ÷ 3" the '''dividend''' is the 42.}}
# {{lb|en|figuratively}} {{U|beneficial}} [[result]]s from a [[metaphorical]] [[investment]] (of [[time]], [[effort]], etc.)
#: {{ux|en|His 10,000 hours of practice and recitals eventually paid '''dividends''' when he become first-chair violinist.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|title=Slow Burn: Dead Fire, Book 4:|url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=1499118910|author=Bobby Adair |year=2014|passage=The money I'd spent on getting scuba certified was about to pay a dividend. My half-baked escape plan came together.}}
#* {{RQ:en:CNN|author=Frida Ghitis|title=The GOP’s xenophobia is fueling toxic culture of hate|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/03/19/opinions/xenophobia-republicans-anti-asian-american-crimes-ghitis|date=2021-03-19|passage=The United States is not the only country where xenophobia pays '''dividends''' for politicians.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220706000750/https://www.cnn.com/2021/03/19/opinions/xenophobia-republicans-anti-asian-american-crimes-ghitis/|archivedate=6 July 2022}}

===Etymology===

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/əˈdɑp.ʃən/|a=GA}}
* {{IPA|en|/əˈdɒp.ʃən/|a=RP}}
* {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Vealhurl-adoption.wav|a=Southern England}}
* {{hyph|en|adop|tion}}

===Noun===
{{en-noun|~}}

# The act of [[adopt]]ing.
# {{senseid|en|Q180472}} The state of being adopted; the acceptance of a child of other parents as if they were one's own child.
#: {{ux|en|A Chinese baby girl was given away for '''adoption'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|Another Chinese boy was put up for '''adoption'''.}}
#* {{RQ:Orczy Miss Elliott|chapter=The Tragedy in Dartmoor Terrace|passage=“The story of this '''adoption''' is, of course, the pivot round which all the circumstances of the mysterious tragedy revolved. Mrs. Yule had an only son, namely, William, to whom she was passionately attached ; but, like many a fond mother, she had the desire of mapping out that son's future entirely according to her own ideas.{{nb...}}”}}
# An admission to an institution, for example a hospital, clinic, mental asylum.
#: {{co|en|the '''adoption''' of people into hospitals or monasteries}}
# The choosing and making that to be one's own which originally was not so; acceptance. 
#: {{co|en|the '''adoption''' of opinions}}
#: {{co|en|the '''adoption''' of words from another language}}
## The act of [[accept]]ing and putting into [[effect]] or [[practice]] (a method, proposal, technique, etc.)
##: {{ux|en|Our company is considering the '''adoption''' of a four-day week.}}
# {{lb|en|computing}} The transfer from an old system to another (usually better) system. {{rfusex|en}}
# {{lb|en|theology}} An act of divine grace by which the redeemed in Christ are admitted to the privileges of the sons of God.
# {{lb|en|chess|slang}} Ten [[consecutive]] [[win]]s against an [[opponent]].
#: {{ux|en|Infuriated by his '''adoption''' yesterday, the chess master has resolved to study twice as long and twice as hard.}}
